title: 2023 budget confirmation with 4.46 per cent levy increase
subtitle: Affordable housing funding, free youth transit, welcoming streets, business supports, Bill 23 impacts and infrastructure levy cut
overview: Council confirmed the 2023 operating budget with a property tax levy increase of 4.46 per cent, down from the 4.96 per cent staff proposed {{vote:m25}}. The budget is the second year of the multi-year cycle. Staff said inflation and supply chain pressures would be offset by temporary surpluses, with any shortfall covered from contingency reserves.

Council added several items, mostly paid from the tax rate contingency reserve. These include $500,000 for the affordable housing reserve {{vote:m7}}, an extension of the Kids Ride Free pilot {{vote:m9}}, and making the sliding-scale bus pass permanent {{vote:m10}}. Council also made funding for the Welcoming Streets downtown outreach program ongoing {{vote:m13}} and added $300,000 for business service agencies {{vote:m15}}.

To offset these additions, council cut the infrastructure renewal transfer by $1.4 million {{vote:m24}}. It voted down proposals to remove phase-in costs for the south end recreation centre and new central library. It also directed staff to assess gaps in housing, homelessness and mental health services {{vote:m16}}. Council asked senior governments for emergency funding {{vote:m27}}. Pickleball facilities and a Dovercliffe Park master plan were referred to the 2024 budget process.

decisions.detail: Council approved the amended budget with a 4.46 per cent levy increase over 2022, along with the capital budget and related reserve decisions {{vote:m25}}.
Council reversed the proposed elimination of the $500,000 transfer and funded it for 2023 from the tax rate operating contingency reserve.
The sliding-scale bus pass pilot becomes ongoing, adding $458,000 a year to the base budget from 2024, with 2023 costs of $558,000 paid from contingency.
The pilot is extended through 2023 until the transit fare strategy is approved, at up to $138,911 from the contingency reserve.
Council approved an ongoing annual contribution of $202,500 for the downtown outreach program, adding 0.07 per cent to the 2023 levy.
Council added $300,000 for business service agency agreements, with a 0.11 per cent levy impact {{vote:m15}}.
Council funded $500,000 of the 2023 financial impacts of Bill 23 from the tax rate operating contingency reserve {{vote:m19}}.
The 2023 infrastructure renewal transfer was reduced by $1.4 million, lowering the overall increase by 0.50 per cent {{vote:m24}}.

debate: On the affordable housing reserve, supporters said local seed money helps non-profit builders leverage provincial and federal funds and that the effects of Bill 23 are still unclear. Staff recommended removing the transfer because Bill 23 exempts affordable housing from development charges. Council funded it one-time from contingency.

On Bill 23, one councillor argued the province may soften its impact and proposed using contingency. Others warned that using reserves for an ongoing cost only defers the increase to later years. Staff said the reserve balance was about $15.7 million and that Bill 23 losses could well exceed the $1 million budgeted.

Delegates from the mental health, outreach and business communities asked for more investment. One councillor questioned whether the city is taking on provincial and county responsibilities. Others said the city needs its own picture of gaps and funding options.

Councillors who wanted to remove phase-in costs for the south end recreation centre and library said residents would not understand paying years before opening. Others said phasing in avoids a later spike and supports planning. Those motions were defeated.

On infrastructure renewal, one councillor said the pace of increases is unaffordable for households. Others and staff said deferring work raises future costs, and a roughly $290 million water backlog was mentioned. Council settled on a smaller cut of $1.4 million.
